script.t: My guest today is Professor Daniel Okoro, who has spent the last twenty years researching what makes people happy. Daniel, let's start with the obvious question. Does money buy happiness?

It's the question everyone asks, and the answer is more nuanced than either 'yes' or 'no'. Up to a certain point, more money clearly does make people happier, because it removes the stress of not being able to pay the rent or feed your family. Beyond that point, the effect becomes much weaker. A famous study suggested the effect levelled off completely at a certain income, although more recent research indicates it continues to rise slowly. What's clear is that a pay rise makes a far bigger difference to someone struggling than to someone who's already comfortable.
So if not money, what does make the biggest difference?

Relationships, by a considerable margin. The longest study of adult life ever conducted, which followed a group of men from Harvard and a group from poor neighbourhoods in Boston for over eighty years, found that the quality of people's relationships was the strongest predictor not only of their happiness, but also of their physical health in old age. People who were more connected to family, friends and community lived longer and were less likely to suffer memory decline. Loneliness, on the other hand, turned out to be as harmful as smoking.
That's quite a claim.

It is, and of course correlation isn't causation. Healthier people may find it easier to maintain friendships. But experimental studies support the idea that social connection itself has a powerful effect. Even brief, casual interactions matter. In one experiment, people who were asked to chat with the barista when buying their coffee, rather than being as efficient as possible, reported feeling noticeably happier afterwards.
What about the things people usually think will make them happy, a bigger house, a promotion?

Here we run into something psychologists call hedonic adaptation. We adjust remarkably quickly to improvements in our circumstances. The new house or the new car gives us a boost, but within months it becomes the new normal and our happiness returns more or less to where it was. Interestingly, research suggests that we adapt more slowly to experiences than to possessions. A holiday or a concert with friends tends to produce longer-lasting satisfaction than a new gadget, partly because we keep retelling the story and partly because experiences are often shared with others.
Is there anything practical people can do?

Several things have reasonably good evidence. Spending money on other people rather than yourself reliably increases happiness, even in small amounts. Regular physical activity helps, as does getting enough sleep. And, although it sounds simplistic, writing down a few things you're grateful for each week seems to have a modest but real effect. What doesn't work, ironically, is trying too hard to be happy. Studies show that people who place enormous value on happiness often end up feeling more disappointed, because they're constantly monitoring whether they've achieved it.
So the secret is not to look for it?

I'd put it slightly differently. Happiness tends to be a by-product of living a life that feels meaningful and connected, rather than a goal you can pursue directly. If you focus on the people and activities you care about, happiness usually follows.

questions.prompt: What does the professor say about money and happiness?
options: Money has no effect on happiness
More money matters most to those who are struggling
The effect stops completely at a fixed income

According to the study, loneliness was as harmful as:

options: Short friendly conversations make people happier

questions.prompt: What do psychologists call our tendency to get used to improvements? (1–3 words)

options: It comes indirectly from a meaningful, connected life

script.t: A biotechnology company recently announced that it aims to bring back a version of the woolly mammoth within the next decade. With me are geneticist Dr Laura Chen, and Richard Hale, a conservation biologist. Laura, is this actually possible?

In a limited sense, yes. We can't clone a mammoth, because no intact living cells survive; even the best-preserved frozen specimens have badly damaged DNA. What scientists propose instead is to take the genome of the Asian elephant, which is the mammoth's closest living relative, and edit it to include the genes responsible for key mammoth traits: thick hair, small ears, a layer of fat to cope with the cold. The result would be a cold-resistant elephant that looks and behaves somewhat like a mammoth. Whether you call that a mammoth is partly a philosophical question. It would certainly not be the same animal that walked across Siberia ten thousand years ago, and nobody serious claims it would be.
And why would anyone want to do this?

The company argues there's an ecological reason. Before they disappeared, mammoths helped maintain the Arctic grasslands by trampling snow and knocking down trees. Today much of that landscape has become forest or moss, and the frozen ground beneath it, the permafrost, is melting and releasing large amounts of greenhouse gases. The theory is that herds of these animals could help restore the grasslands and keep the ground colder.
Richard, you're sceptical.

Very. Let me be clear, the science is fascinating, and I don't doubt the good intentions of many people involved. But the climate argument doesn't stand up to scrutiny. To have any meaningful effect on the permafrost, you'd need hundreds of thousands of animals spread across an area larger than many countries. Elephants reproduce extremely slowly, with a pregnancy of almost two years. We're talking about centuries, not decades, and by then the permafrost problem will have been decided one way or another.

That's a fair point about the timescale, but the research could have other benefits. The same gene-editing techniques might help endangered species today, for example by making Asian elephants resistant to a virus that kills many of their young.

I'd support that kind of work wholeheartedly. My concern is about priorities and money. Every year, we lose species that we could save with relatively cheap, proven measures, protecting habitats, stopping poaching. Spending enormous sums on bringing back an animal that's been extinct for four thousand years sends a dangerous message: that extinction is reversible, so we needn't worry so much about it.
There's also an animal welfare question, isn't there?

Absolutely. Elephants are intelligent, highly social animals. The first calf would be born, presumably to an artificial womb or a surrogate elephant mother, with no herd of its own kind to learn from. What sort of life would that be?

Those are serious ethical issues and they need public debate before anything goes ahead. But I don't think we should stop the research. Many technologies we now take for granted started as projects that seemed like science fiction.
I agree they need debate. I'd just rather we spent our energy keeping the elephants we have.

questions.prompt: Why can't scientists simply clone a mammoth?
What would the 'mammoth' actually be, according to Dr Chen?
options: An exact copy of a mammoth
A modified elephant with mammoth traits

questions.prompt: What frozen ground is releasing greenhouse gases? (1–3 words)

options: It would take far too long to have enough animals
There is no permafrost in the Arctic

options: That climate change is not real

questions.prompt: On what do the two experts finally agree?
options: The ethical issues need public discussion
The mammoth will help the climate

script.t: Today we're looking at how companies use psychology to influence what we pay. Let's begin with something you've all seen: prices ending in ninety-nine. Why do shops charge nine ninety-nine rather than ten? Rationally, the difference is trivial. But research consistently shows that it affects sales, a phenomenon known as the left-digit effect. We read from left to right, and our brains give disproportionate weight to the first digit. So nine ninety-nine is perceived as 'nine-something', which feels significantly cheaper than ten. Interestingly, luxury brands often avoid this strategy deliberately. A designer handbag will be priced at exactly two thousand, because round numbers signal quality and confidence, rather than a bargain. A second technique is what's called anchoring. The first number we see strongly influences our judgement of what follows. Restaurants sometimes put one extremely expensive dish at the top of the menu, not because they expect to sell many, but because it makes everything else look reasonable by comparison. Similarly, a jacket labelled 'was two hundred, now one twenty' seems like a great deal, even if it was never actually sold at the original price. Then there's the decoy effect, which I find particularly clever. A famous example involved a magazine that offered three subscription options: online only for fifty-nine dollars, print only for a hundred and twenty-five, and print plus online, also for a hundred and twenty-five. Obviously, nobody chose the print-only option. But its presence made the combined package look like an incredible bargain. When researchers removed the decoy, far more people chose the cheaper online-only option. In other words, an option that nobody wants can still change what everybody buys. Companies selling coffee, cinema snacks and mobile phone contracts use exactly the same trick, which is why the medium size is often priced suspiciously close to the large.
Sorry, can I ask something? Isn't that a bit manipulative? Is it even legal?

Good question. Most of these techniques are perfectly legal, because the information is accurate; it's the presentation that's being designed. Where it becomes illegal, in many countries, is when the information itself is false, for example, claiming a reference price that never existed. Regulators have become much stricter about fake discounts in recent years. Whether it's ethical is a separate debate, and that's actually what your essay this term will be about.
So how can consumers protect themselves?

Awareness helps, although less than we'd like to think; these effects work even on people who know about them. A few practical strategies, though. Decide what something is worth to you before you look at the price. Compare the price per unit, per kilo or per litre, rather than per package. And be particularly suspicious of time pressure, those countdown clocks on websites telling you an offer ends in ten minutes. Urgency is designed to stop you thinking carefully. One more technique before we finish, and it's one that subscription services love: making it easy to start and difficult to stop. Free trials that automatically turn into paid subscriptions rely on the fact that most people forget to cancel. Some companies make the cancellation process deliberately complicated, a practice now targeted by new consumer laws. For next week, I'd like you each to find three real examples of these techniques, online or in shops, and analyse how they work.

options: They suggest quality rather than a bargain

options: To make other dishes seem reasonably priced

script.t: Isabel Moreno's latest novel, The Salt Road, has just been shortlisted for a major literary prize. Isabel, congratulations. This is your fourth novel, but you didn't publish your first until you were forty-five. Why so late?

Thank you. Well, I'd been writing in secret for years, mostly in the early mornings before going to my job as a hospital pharmacist. I wrote three complete novels that nobody will ever read, and rightly so. They were apprentice work. I think I needed that time, not just to learn the craft, but to have lived enough to have something to say. I sometimes envy writers who publish brilliant debuts at twenty-five, but I don't think I could have written this book without the experiences of the last twenty years.
The Salt Road follows three generations of a family in a fishing village in Galicia. How much of it is autobiographical?

Less than people assume. My grandmother did come from a village like that, and some of her stories found their way into the book, but the characters are invented. What's autobiographical, I suppose, is the emotional landscape: the sense of a community that's disappearing, of young people leaving, of a language spoken at home but not at school. Those are things I grew up with. My mother still speaks Galician to me on the phone, even though we both live in Madrid now, and I think the book is partly a love letter to that language.
Can you describe your writing process?

It's chaotic, I'm afraid. Some writers plan everything before they start, chapter by chapter. I've tried, and it doesn't work for me. If I know exactly what's going to happen, I lose interest. I usually start with an image. For The Salt Road it was an old woman mending a net on a beach, refusing to look at the sea. I didn't know why she refused, and the novel was really my attempt to find out. The disadvantage of working this way is that I have to rewrite enormously. The first draft of this book was almost twice as long as the final version. Whole characters disappeared.
Is that painful?

At first it was agonising. Now I see it as part of the process. A first draft is just you telling yourself the story. The second and third drafts are where you work out how to tell it to someone else. My editor is wonderful at pointing out where I've fallen in love with a beautiful sentence that isn't actually doing anything.
What advice would you give to people who are writing in secret, as you were?

Two things. First, read much more than you write, and read like a writer, asking yourself how an author creates a particular effect. Second, finish things. So many talented people have dozens of brilliant opening chapters in a drawer. You learn far more from completing a bad novel than from starting ten good ones. The ending is where you discover what the book is about.
And what are you working on now?
I never talk about work in progress. It's a superstition. If I explain the story aloud, I seem to lose the need to write it.

options: She thinks her life experience was necessary for her book
She thinks young writers are better

options: The emotional atmosphere of a disappearing community

title: Antibiotic resistance
model: Cambridge C1 Advanced – Listening Part 2/3 (radio feature)

script.t: When penicillin became widely available in the 1940s, it transformed medicine. Infections that had routinely killed people, from pneumonia to infected cuts, could suddenly be cured in days. But that golden age may be coming to an end. Dr Samuel Price is a microbiologist. Samuel, how serious is the problem of antibiotic resistance?

Extremely serious, and I don't say that lightly. It's estimated that drug-resistant infections already directly cause more than a million deaths a year worldwide, and contribute to several million more. If current trends continue, some projections suggest that by 2050 they could kill more people each year than cancer does today. We are already seeing patients with infections for which no antibiotic works at all.
How does resistance develop?

It's evolution in action. When you take an antibiotic, it kills most of the bacteria causing the infection. But within any population of bacteria, there may be a few with random genetic mutations that allow them to survive. Those survivors then multiply, and the next generation is resistant. Bacteria can also share resistance genes with each other, even between different species, which accelerates the process enormously. Some bacteria can divide every twenty minutes, so in a single day an enormous number of generations can appear, each one a new opportunity for resistance to develop. The more we use antibiotics, the more opportunities we give resistant bacteria to take over.
So we're using them too much?

In many cases, yes. One major problem is prescribing antibiotics for viral infections, such as colds and most sore throats, where they're completely useless, because antibiotics don't work against viruses. Patients often expect a prescription, and busy doctors sometimes give in. Another problem is people stopping a course early because they feel better, although the advice on that is actually changing; for some infections, shorter courses are now recommended. But by far the largest use is in agriculture. In many countries, more antibiotics are given to farm animals than to humans, often not to treat illness but to prevent it in crowded conditions or to make animals grow faster.
Why aren't pharmaceutical companies developing new antibiotics?

That's the uncomfortable economic paradox. Developing a new antibiotic costs over a billion dollars and takes more than a decade. But when a new one is approved, doctors are told to use it as little as possible, keeping it in reserve for the most serious cases, precisely to slow down resistance. So sales are tiny, and companies can't recover their investment. Several small firms that successfully developed new antibiotics have actually gone bankrupt. Governments are now experimenting with new payment models, paying companies a fixed annual fee for access to an antibiotic regardless of how much is used, a bit like a subscription.
Is there anything ordinary people can do?

Quite a lot, actually. Don't pressure your doctor for antibiotics, and never take leftover ones or share them with others. Wash your hands properly and keep up to date with vaccinations, because preventing an infection is better than treating it. And as consumers, we can support farming that uses antibiotics responsibly. None of this sounds dramatic, but collectively it makes a real difference.

options: Resistant infections could kill more people than cancer does today

script.t: I'm joined by Grace and Owen, a couple who, three years ago, sold their three-bedroom house and moved into a tiny home of just twenty-two square metres. Grace, what made you do it?

Honestly, it started as a financial decision. We had a huge mortgage, we were both working long hours to pay for it, and we realised we were spending most of our lives earning money for a house we hardly had time to enjoy. One evening we sat down and calculated that if we sold it and built a tiny home, we'd be completely debt-free. That was a very powerful idea. We spent about a year visiting other tiny homes, talking to the people who lived in them and reading everything we could find before we made the final decision.
Owen, was it difficult to get rid of so many things?

Much harder than I expected, emotionally rather than practically. We gave away or sold about eighty per cent of what we owned. The books were the worst for me. I'd been collecting them since I was a teenager. In the end I kept about fifty and gave the rest to the local library. But here's the strange thing: after about a month, I couldn't remember most of what we'd got rid of. It felt incredibly liberating.
For me, the hardest part was the clothes. I had a wardrobe full of things I'd bought and worn maybe twice. Now everything I own fits in two drawers, and I spend no time at all deciding what to wear.
What about living together in such a small space? Don't you get on each other's nerves?

We were worried about that. And the first winter was a real test, because we couldn't spend much time outside. We had a few arguments. But we've developed rules. For example, if one of us needs time alone, the other goes for a walk, no questions asked. And we designed the space carefully, so there's a little reading corner and a desk that folds away.
I'd also say it forced us to communicate better. In a big house, you can avoid problems by going to different rooms. Here, you have to deal with things.
Are there any downsides you didn't anticipate?

Legal ones. Planning regulations in many places weren't designed for homes like ours, and finding land where we were allowed to live permanently took almost a year. We now rent a corner of a farm. Also, it's difficult to have guests. When Grace's parents visit, they stay in a bed and breakfast in the village.

And I do miss having a bath sometimes! But overall, the benefits far outweigh the disadvantages. Because we have no mortgage, I've reduced my working hours to three days a week, and Owen has started his own furniture business, which he could never have risked before.
Would you recommend it to others?

Not for everyone, certainly not for a big family. But I'd recommend that everyone asks the question we asked: how much space and how many things do I really need, and what am I giving up to pay for them?

script.t: We tend to think of time as something fixed and natural, but the way we measure it is a surprisingly recent social invention. Until the mid-nineteenth century, almost every town set its clocks by the sun. Noon was simply the moment when the sun was highest in the sky. Since the sun moves across the sky from east to west, this meant that noon in Bristol, in the west of England, came about ten minutes later than noon in London. Nobody minded, because travel between towns was slow. If it took you two days to make the journey by coach, a ten-minute difference was irrelevant. In fact, most people never travelled more than a few kilometres from the place where they were born, so the question of what time it was in another town simply never arose. The railways changed everything. Suddenly people could travel hundreds of kilometres in a day, and train companies needed to publish timetables. If every station used its own local time, the timetables became extraordinarily confusing, and there was a real risk of accidents on lines where trains travelled in both directions on the same track. In Britain, the railway companies solved the problem in the 1840s by adopting London time, also called Greenwich Mean Time, across the whole network. Many towns resisted at first. Some public clocks had two minute hands, one showing local time and one showing railway time. Exeter's cathedral authorities were famously reluctant to accept what they saw as London imposing its time on them. But by the 1850s, most of the country had accepted railway time, although it only became legally standard in 1880. The problem was much greater in the United States, which is so wide that a single national time made no sense. By the early 1880s, American railways were using around fifty different times. In 1883, the railway companies, without waiting for the government, divided the country into four time zones. The day they switched became known as 'the day of two noons', because in many places clocks had to be put back, so noon happened twice. The following year, an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the prime meridian, the zero point from which longitude and the world's time zones would be measured.
Why Greenwich, and not Paris, for example?

Good question, and the French certainly asked it! The main reason was practical: by then, around seventy per cent of the world's shipping already used sea charts based on Greenwich, so it caused the least disruption. France abstained from the vote, and continued to use Paris time for several more decades. Of course, it also reflected Britain's power at the time.
So time zones are partly political?

Very much so, and they still are. China, which is as wide as the continental United States, uses one single time zone, for reasons of national unity. In the far west of the country, that means the sun can rise as late as ten in the morning. And countries change their zones for political or economic reasons surprisingly often. So the next time you look at your watch, remember that the number it shows is as much a product of history as of astronomy.

script.t: Dr Arjun Mehta leads a robotics laboratory that builds machines that can walk on two legs. Arjun, robots can now beat world champions at chess. Why is walking still so hard?

It's what we call Moravec's paradox, named after a robotics researcher. Things humans find difficult, like advanced mathematics or chess, are relatively easy for computers, while things a toddler does without thinking, walking, picking up a cup, recognising a face, are extremely hard. The reason is that evolution has spent hundreds of millions of years perfecting our movement. It happens so automatically that we don't realise how complex it is. When you walk, you're constantly falling forward and catching yourself, making tiny adjustments hundreds of times a second based on information from your eyes, your inner ear and thousands of sensors in your muscles and feet.
So how do you teach a robot to do that?

For decades, engineers tried to write precise mathematical rules for every movement. That works reasonably well on flat, predictable surfaces, a factory floor, for instance. But the real world is messy. Grass, gravel, ice, stairs, a dog running across your path. You simply can't write rules for every situation. The big change in recent years has been machine learning. Instead of programming the robot, we create a simulated version of it in a computer and let it practise walking millions of times in a virtual world, with randomly changing ground, wind and obstacles. It falls over constantly at first, but gradually learns what works. Then we transfer that learning to the physical robot.
Does it work immediately in the real world?

Rarely. We call it the reality gap. A simulation is never perfect; real motors heat up, real ground is slightly springier than the computer predicted. So the robot usually stumbles at first. The trick is to make the simulation deliberately unpredictable, so the robot learns to cope with uncertainty in general rather than with one specific virtual world. When we did that, our robot learned to walk on a frozen lake on its very first attempt, which honestly amazed the whole team. Nobody had ever shown it ice in training. It had simply learned to expect the unexpected, which is exactly what animals do.
Why build robots with legs at all? Wheels seem much simpler.

Wheels are wonderful on roads. But much of the world, and almost every building, is designed for legs. Think of stairs, narrow doorways, rubble after an earthquake. The applications we're most excited about are in disaster response, searching collapsed buildings where it's too dangerous to send people, and in inspecting places like offshore wind turbines or nuclear facilities.
Some people find humanoid robots rather frightening. Do you understand that?

Completely. Science fiction hasn't done us many favours! And there are legitimate concerns about jobs and about military use, which the research community needs to take seriously. Personally, I've signed a pledge not to work on weapons. But I'd say that, having watched our robots fall over thousands of times, it's quite hard to see them as a threat. Most days, they're more like clumsy toddlers than terminators.

options: It requires constant tiny adjustments based on many senses

script.t: Several schools in our area have recently abolished homework for younger pupils. Katherine Lloyd is head teacher of one of them; James Porter is a secondary school maths teacher who disagrees. Katherine, why did you do it?

We looked carefully at the research, and for primary-age children, the evidence that homework improves learning is surprisingly weak. For teenagers, there's a moderate benefit, but for children under about eleven, it seems to make very little difference to achievement. What it does do, quite often, is cause stress and arguments at home. And it increases inequality. A child whose parents have time, education and a quiet room to offer gets far more out of homework than a child whose parents work evenings or don't speak English well. So we were adding to the gap rather than closing it.
James, you're not convinced.

I accept the point about inequality, and I think Katherine's school has made a reasonable decision for very young children. My concern is when this becomes a general movement against homework, including for older students. In my subject, practice is essential. You can't learn mathematics by watching someone else do it, any more than you can learn to swim by watching. And the students who struggle most are often the ones who need the most repetition before a method becomes automatic. There simply isn't enough time in lessons for the amount of practice students need.

I'd agree that practice matters. But much traditional homework isn't well designed. Thirty identical questions don't help a student who didn't understand the method; they just practise the mistake thirty times. In a recent survey at my school, many parents also said they had no idea how to help with homework, because methods have changed since they were at school. And a student who already understands learns nothing from them.

That's a criticism of bad homework, not of homework itself. Good homework is short, focused and gets feedback. For example, I set ten minutes of retrieval practice, students try to answer questions on topics we covered weeks or months ago. Research on memory shows that's one of the most effective learning techniques there is. It doesn't take long, students can do it on the bus, and I can see straight away which topics they have forgotten.
What about the inequality argument, James?

It's real, but abolishing homework isn't the only answer. Our school runs a homework club every afternoon in the library, with teachers available to help. Students who don't have a quiet space at home can work there. That seems better than removing the opportunity altogether.

I think that's an excellent idea, and if we had the funding, we'd consider it. What we've done instead is encourage families to read together every evening, and that's the one thing we still ask for. The research on reading for pleasure is very strong.
Has abolishing homework affected your results?

It's early to say, after just two years, but our results have stayed the same, and the children's reported wellbeing has improved significantly. Teachers also have more time to plan lessons, because they're not marking homework every evening.
Well, if results haven't fallen, that's an interesting finding. I'd want to see what happens when those children reach secondary school, though.

options: It has little effect on achievement

options: Some children have more support at home than others

options: Students need more practice than lessons allow

title: The secret life of the deep ocean

script.t: More than half of our planet's surface lies under water over three thousand metres deep. It is a world of total darkness, near-freezing temperatures and crushing pressure, hundreds of times greater than at the surface. For centuries, scientists assumed that nothing could live there. In the nineteenth century, one respected naturalist even declared that life was impossible below about five hundred metres. We now know how wrong he was. Dr Felix Andersson is a deep-sea biologist.

Every time we send a submersible to the deep sea floor, we find species that are new to science. On some expeditions, the majority of animals we collect have never been described before. We've explored a smaller proportion of the deep ocean than of the surface of Mars, which I find remarkable. And the creatures are extraordinary. Around three quarters of deep-sea animals produce their own light, a process called bioluminescence. They use it to attract prey, to find mates, or to confuse predators. Some fish have huge eyes to catch the tiniest flashes of light; others have lost their eyes completely.

One of the most surprising discoveries came in 1977, when scientists exploring near the Galápagos Islands found hydrothermal vents, cracks in the sea floor where volcanic heat warms the water to over three hundred and fifty degrees Celsius. Around them were entire communities of life: giant tube worms two metres long, clams, crabs and shrimp, living in complete darkness.

That discovery changed biology. Until then, it was believed that virtually all life on Earth ultimately depended on the sun, through photosynthesis. But these communities depend on bacteria that obtain energy from chemicals coming out of the vents, a process called chemosynthesis. Some scientists now think life on Earth may actually have begun in places like these, and it has made researchers more optimistic about finding life on moons such as Europa, which may have oceans beneath their ice.

But this hidden world now faces a new threat. The deep sea floor is covered in places by potato-sized lumps called nodules, rich in metals such as cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are essential for the batteries in electric cars. Several companies are pushing to begin mining them on an industrial scale.

This is a genuine dilemma. We need these metals for the transition away from fossil fuels, and mining on land also causes serious environmental and human damage. But the deep sea recovers incredibly slowly. In an experiment in the Pacific in 1989, scientists ploughed a small area of the sea floor to simulate mining. When they returned twenty-six years later, many species still hadn't returned. And the nodules themselves take millions of years to form, and they're the habitat for many organisms. Once they're gone, they're gone. My view is that we simply don't know enough yet to mine responsibly. Many scientists, and an increasing number of governments and car manufacturers, are calling for a pause until we do. That doesn't mean never. It means doing the basic science first, so that if mining does go ahead, we understand the risks and can set strict rules.
The future of the deep ocean, it seems, may be decided before we have even discovered most of what lives there.
